text.body:
An Introductory Comment
This final pair of sermons presents a unique case in the Wesley corpus. What we have here is one sermon on the same text, in two versions (one in English, the other in Latin). They are so nearly alike that one is tempted to suppose that we are dealing with an instance of translation. They are, however, different enough to suggest a single project in two different drafts. What little we know of the actual circumstances supports this latter conjecture.
As one of the twelve Fellows of Lincoln College, Wesley had been expected to proceed to the degree of Bachelor of Divinity within seven years after his Master of Arts degree (1727). The reasons for his failure to do this are not clear. At any rate, in 1736, while he was in Georgia, he was elected to the only fellowship in the college (the so-called ‘canonist fellowship’) exempted from the B.D. requirement. Moreover, he continued to hold this fellowship, at considerable inconvenience to the college, until his resignation in 1751.
That Wesley remained mindful of the expectations of his college, even after his forsaking it for his new role in the Revival, can be seen in an aside in a letter written from Bristol, October 27, 1739, to his brother Samuel in Tiverton. His main interest in this letter is a sprightly defence of his new career against his brother’s sharp criticisms of it. But he also adds the following bit of ‘news’:
In a few days, my [younger] brother and I are to go to Oxford to do exercise for our [B.D.] degrees. Then, if God enables me, I will prove my charge [of works-righteousness] against Bishop [George] Bull, either in my Latin sermon, or Supposition Speech.
No mention is made of this in the Journal, but it is recorded there that John and Charles turned up in Oxford on November 12. However, three days later, the belated news of their brother’s sudden death (November 5) came to them, and they immediately set out for Tiverton.
JWJ, November 20-24, 1739. For a time, with the excitements and demands of the burgeoning Revival, the matter of an academic degree drops out of John’s sight. And yet, despite his absence from Oxford and his mounting public notice, the
university officials were still prepared to invite him to take his regular turn as preacher to the university—this time on July 25, 1741 (i.e., during ‘Long Vacation’, when the majority of the dons and students would be absent). He seems to have regarded such an invitation as a twofold opportunity: to deal with his own academic arrears respecting that deferred B.D., and also to deliver a long-considered diatribe against the university as a whole, on the charge of its manifold lapses in doctrine and discipline. The Journal entry for June 18 confirms this:
I inquired concerning the exercises previous to the degree of Bachelor of Divinity; and advised with Mr. Gambold concerning the subject of my sermon before the university; but he seemed to think it of no moment. ‘For’, said he, ‘all here are so prejudiced that they will mind nothing you say.’ I know that. However, I am to deliver my own soul, whether they will hear or whether they will forebear.
Incidentally, though, this exchange with Gambold, with other things, seems to have led to a rupture, for the Journal entry for July 2 reports matter-of-factly: ‘I met Mr. Gambold again, who honestly told me he was ashamed of my company.’
On this visit to Oxford, he had returned again to his ‘charge against Bishop Bull’
JWJ, June 24, 1741. by re-reading the latter’s Harmonia Apostolica—ignoring Robert Nelson’s careful explanation that Bull’s doctrine of justification was not Pelagian.
Nelson, The Life of Dr. George Bull (1714), pp. 95-99. And, even earlier (June 19, according to the diary), Wesley had ‘writ plan of sermon’ on the same day that he had ‘read the Canons of the Council of Trent’. It was, therefore, a time of theological reading and reflection, as if in ‘cramming’ for an examination.
Wesley’s diary indicates that he was also writing three Latin exercises (geneses), on predestination, on the means of grace, and on justification, presumably to satisfy the lecture requirement for the degree (JWJ, June 20, 1741); see G. R. M. Ward, Oxford University Statutes (Oxford, 1848), I:55. Cf. JW MS ‘S. Paulus per totum 7m ad Rom. caput…’ (number ‘3’ at the top), in MA. On the 22nd, there is a note that he had written out a ‘plan of Latin sermon’ (i.e., one of the B.D. exercises).
The Statutes (Tit. VI.6.2) required that a person standing for admission to the degree of Bachelor of Divinity ‘preach in his own person, and not by deputy, a Latin sermon in the church of St. Mary the Virgin’. Ward, Statutes, I:55. These scattered bits of evidence allow for the conjecture that he was preparing a sermon for St. Mary’s in which he could ‘deliver his soul’ and also satisfy one of the B.D. requirements.
As far as we know, nothing came of this plan. Apparently, Wesley was dissuaded from preaching the sermon on Isa. 1:21 in St. Mary’s (and by Lady Huntingdon, no less). And there is no record of his ever having
submitted anything officially for that B.D. degree. Instead, for the university sermon on July 25 he wrote out a different piece, on a text he had tried before, on Acts 26:28 (see No. 2, The Almost Christian). And when he returned to St. Mary’s for the last time in 1744 (see No. 4, Scriptural Christianity), he couched his denunciation of the university in very different terms.
It is all the more remarkable, therefore, that Wesley took the necessary pains to preserve both the English and Latin holographs of these two unpreached sermons. The manuscript in English that is transcribed here exists in nineteen numbered duodecimo pages now in the Colman Miscellany in the Methodist Archives, Manchester. After Wesley’s death, it passed into John Pawson’s possession and was published in 1797 in the Arminian Magazine
XX.265-69, 317-22. with a misleading foreword by Adam Clarke:
The following sermon was found in a mutilated manuscript among Mr. Wesley’s papers. It is dated June 24, 1741. A Latin copy of the same discourse has also been discovered. Mr. Pawson, with great care, copied the former, and I have supplied the deficiencies out of the latter. On collating both sermons, I find several variations, and though not of any great importance, yet sufficient, in my judgment, to vindicate the propriety of translating and publishing the Latin one, not merely as a matter of curiosity, but of utility. The sermon, no doubt, was written with the design of being preached before the University of Oxford, but whether it ever were preached there, cannot be determined.
The English text was then reproduced by Joseph Benson in his edition of the Works,
(1812), XI.72-85. with minor alterations and one major addition in I.7 (three paragraphs added from the Latin). Benson also supplied it with its triumphalist title, ‘True Christianity Defended’. Thomas Jackson followed Benson faithfully in both title and text.
The holograph of the Latin sermon, dated by Wesley June 27, 1741 (three days after the English version), has also survived; it is in the Morley Collection in Wesley College, Bristol. It is the most extensive example we have of Wesley’s prowess with neo-Ciceronian Latin—an impressive reminder of his grounding in the classics at Charterhouse and Christ Church. The English version here follows Wesley’s own holograph. The Latin version is presented here for the first time: its orthography has been modernized, with Wesley’s abbreviations fitted out (e.g., the enclitic -que which he regularly shortens to -q at the endings of conjunctive nouns), and a few obvious lapses have been corrected silently. It is placed here in sequence to the English text, with its [04:392]own annotation, so that either version may be read separately and yet also compared with the other. For the English text, a few notes are offered (besides the usual annotations) calling attention to significant omissions, or variations between it and its Latin counterpart. In the transcription of the latter, and in the notes on various peculiarities of Wesley’s vocabulary and syntax, I have had the generous help of an expert Latinist, Fr. Placid Gilbert, O.S.B. (Cist.), of the Abbey of Our Lady of Dallas (Texas). Sermon 150 Hypocrisy in Oxford Isaiah 1:21 How is the faithful city become an harlot!
1. ‘When I bring the sword upon a land’, saith the Lord, ‘if the watchman blow the trumpet, and warn the people; then whosoever heareth the sound of the trumpet, and taketh not warning, if the sword come and take him away, his blood shall be upon his own head. But if the watchman see the sword come, and blow not the trumpet, and the people be not warned; if the sword come and take any person from among them, he is taken away in his iniquity; but his blood will I require at the watchman’s hand.’
Ezek. 33:2-4, 6; see No. 137, ‘On Corrupting the Word of God’, III.1.
2. It cannot be doubted but that word of the Lord is come unto every minister of Christ also: ‘So thou, O son of man, I have set thee a watchman unto the house of Israel. Therefore thou shalt hear the word at my mouth, and warn them from me. When I say unto the wicked, O wicked man, thou shalt surely die; if thou dost not speak to warn the wicked from his way, that wicked man shall die in his iniquity; but his blood will I require at thine hand.’
Ezek. 33:7-8.
3. Nor ought any man therefore to be counted our enemy, because he telleth us the truth: the doing which is indeed an
instance of love to our neighbour, as well as of obedience to God.
See No. 65, ‘The Duty of Reproving our Neighbour’. Otherwise few would undertake so thankless a task. For the return they will find, they know already—the Scripture must be fulfilled: ‘Me the world hateth; because I testify of them that their deeds are evil.’
[Cf.] John [7:7].
4. It is from a full, settled conviction that I owe this labour of love to my brethren, and to my tender parent,
Alma Mater; i.e., the university of which he had been a member since the summer of 1720. by whom I have been nourished for now more than twenty years, and from whom under God I have received those advantages of which I trust I shall retain a grateful sense till my spirit returns to God that gave it. It is, I say, from a full conviction that love and gratitude, as well as that dispensation of the gospel
See 1 Cor. 9:17. wherewith I am entrusted, require it of me, that even I have undertaken to speak on a needful though unwelcome subject. I could indeed have wished that some more acceptable person would have done this. But should all hold their peace, the very stones would cry out,
See Luke 19:40. ‘How is the faithful city become an harlot!’
5. How faithful she once was to her Lord, to whom she had been betrothed as a chaste virgin, let not only the writings of her sons, which shall be had in honour throughout all generations, but also the blood of her martyrs speak—a stronger testimony of her faithfulness than could be given by words, even
By all the speeches of the babbling earth.
Cf. Prior, ‘Charity’, l. 6: ‘In all the speeches of the babbling earth.’
But how is she now become an harlot! How hath she departed from her Lord! How hath she denied him and listened to the voice of strangers,
See John 10:5. both
I. In respect of doctrine, and
II. Of practice.
I. In respect of doctrine.
1. It cannot indeed be said that all our writers are setters forth [04:394]of strange doctrine.
See Acts 17:18. Wesley had already denounced doctrinal innovation in his earlier university sermon, ‘The Circumcision of the Heart’ (No. 17, §1). Later, he had turned his aversion into an adage, a doctrine ‘wholly new is wholly wrong’; see No. 25, ‘Sermon on the Mount, V’, §1 and n. There are those who expound the oracles of God
See No. 5, ‘Justification by Faith’, §2 and n. by the same Spirit wherewith they were written; and who faithfully cleave to that solid foundation which our Church hath laid agreeably thereto;
E.g., there was Thomas Cockman, Master of University College, who had preached two solidly evangelical sermons before the University of Oxford, Jan. 2 and 6, 1732, Salvation by Jesus Christ Alone, Asserted and Vindicated (against the deists). They are close enough to the soteriology of Wesley’s ‘Circumcision of the Heart’ to warrant a cross-reference (cf. pp. 24-25, 41-43): ‘[After and because of man’s sin] God was himself pleased to find out a way for [men] to escape into the terms of a new and gracious Covenant, whereby God engages himself in consideration of the merits and intercession of our blessed Saviour…and upon condition of certain duties to be performed on man’s part (such as repentance, faith, sincerity of obedience to the law for the time to come [i.e., consequent to forgiveness]…as set forth in Scripture), I say, God engages his faithfulness and justice, upon these conditions “to pardon their transgressions, and their sins and iniquities to remember no more…”. This…is the state of grace and salvation.’ Wesley’s diary shows that he was not in Oxford on Jan. 2 and did not attend the university service on Jan. 6. He had not, therefore, heard two important examples of ‘sound doctrine’ in Oxford. Who knows how many others there may have been? touching which we have his word who cannot lie, that the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.
Matt. 16:18. Note the unconscious triumphalism implied in the claim that the ‘gates of hell shall not prevail against’ the Church of England. There are those also (blessed be the Author of every good gift!) who as wise master-builders build thereon, not hay or stubble, but gold and precious stones,
See 1 Cor. 3:11-12. but that charity which never faileth.
For Wesley’s translation of ἀγάπη, see No. 17, ‘The Circumcision of the Heart’, I.2 and n.
2. We have likewise cause to give thanks to the Father of lights,
Jas. 1:17. for that he hath not yet left himself without witness,
See Acts 14:17. but there are those who now preach the gospel of peace,
Rom. 10:15. the truth as it is in Jesus.
See Eph. 4:21. But how few are these in comparison of those who corrupt the word of God!
2 Cor. 2:17; see his defence of his father in No. 137, ‘On Corrupting the Word of God’; see also No. 36, ‘The Law Established through Faith, II’, I.1 and n. How little wholesome food have we for our souls, and what abundance of poison! How few are there that either in writing or preaching declare the genuine gospel of Christ in that simplicity and purity wherewith it is set forth in the venerable records of our own Church! And how are we enclosed
on every side with those who neither knowing the doctrines of our Church, nor the Scriptures, nor the power of God, have found out to themselves many inventions,
Eccles. 7:29. wherewith they continually corrupt others also!
The following paragraph was first entered here and then deleted: ‘3. To instance only in one or two fundamental points. The doctrine of St. Paul and the Church of England concerning the justification of man is this (Art. XI [‘Of the Justification of Man’]): “We are counted righteous before God—only by faith—and that we are justified by faith only is a most wholesome doctrine.”’
3. I speak not now of those πρωτότοκοι τοῦ Σατανᾶ,
‘The first-born of Satan’; see ‘The Epistle of Polycarp to the Philippians’, VII.1, in The Apostolic Fathers (Loeb, 24:293); see also No. 32, ‘Sermon on the Mount, XII’, I.7 and n. the Deists, Arians, or Socinians. These are too infamous among us to do any great service to the cause of their master. But what shall we say if those whom we have accounted the pillars of our Church, and champions of our faith, do indeed betray that Church, and sap the very foundations of the faith we are taught thereby?
4. But how invidious a thing is it to show this? Who is sufficient to bear the weight of prejudice which must necessarily follow the very mention of such a charge, against men of so established characters? Nay, and who have indeed in many other respects done great service to the Church of God? Yet must every faithful [believer] say, God forbid that I should accept any man’s person.
See Job 32:21. I dare not give any man flattering titles,
See Job 32:21-22; for instances where Wesley asserts that he dare not call any man ‘Rabbi’, see No. 97, ‘On Obedience to Pastors’, II.3 and n. or spare any that corrupts the gospel. In so doing my Maker would soon take me away.
See Job 32:22.
5. Let me, however, be as short as may be on this head. And I will therefore instance only in two or three men of renown who have endeavoured to sap the very foundation of our Church by attacking its fundamental d[octrine], and indeed the fundamental [doctrine]
Cf. Wesley’s letter to his brother Samuel, Jan. 1739, where he lists justification as one ‘of the fundamental Articles of the Church of England’. of all the Reformed Churches, viz., justification by faith alone.
6. One of these, and one of the highest station in our Church, hath wrote and printed before his death several sermons expressly to prove that not faith alone, but good works also, are [04:396]necessary in order to justification.
Here the MS orig. read: ‘good works also must precede justification.’ The unpleasing task of quoting particular passages out of them is superseded by the very title of them, which is this: ‘The Necessity of Regeneration (which he at large proves to imply holiness both of heart and life) in Order to Justification.’
Note Wesley’s invidious rephrasing here of the title of John Tillotson’s five sermons, ‘Of the Nature of Regeneration, and its Necessity in order to Justification and Salvation’, Nos. LII-LVI, in Tillotson’s Works (1722), I.365-94. There is no denying that in these sermons, and generally, Tillotson had espoused the cause of ‘holy living’, but the implication that he also held to a soteriology of ‘works-righteousness’ or ‘self-salvation’ is seriously misleading. Wesley’s distortion is a function of his total preoccupation at the time with his new Moravian view of justification by faith alone as wholly antecedent to regeneration in any sense. Later he would speak of prevenient grace which does not regenerate but which prepares the heart for the gift of justifying faith.
7. It may appear strange to some that an angel of the Church of God
See Rev. 2:1, etc. Tillotson (1630-94) died as Archbishop of Canterbury after three years in that office. These sermons, however, had been written earlier when Tillotson was preacher at Lincoln’s Inn; cf. Irène Simon, Three Restoration Divines (Paris, 1967), I.277-300. Tillotson had been educated at Cambridge and had had no official connection with Oxford. (as the great Shepherd terms the supreme overseers of it), and one so highly esteemed both in our own and many other nations, should coolly and calmly thus speak. But Oh! what is he in comparison of the great Bishop Bull!
Wesley is here stirring embers of a smouldering fire of controversy. George Bull (1634-1710) had studied at Oxford (Exeter College) but had taken no earned degrees from the university. The controversy had erupted in 1669-70 when Bull (then rector of the rural parishes of Suddington St. Mary’s and St. Peter’s, near Cirencester) had published an attempted reconciliation of St. Paul’s sola fide and St. James’s dictum, ‘faith without works is dead,’ in an essay entitled Harmonia Apostolica. It was, in effect, a restatement of the soteriology of Clement of Rome’s Epistle to the Corinthians, that ‘the blood of Christ, poured out for our salvation, brought to the whole world the grace of repentance’ (§7), that the repentant are ‘honoured’, not through themselves or their own works or the holy lives they led, but through [God’s] will (§32). Even so, ‘the Lord himself rejoiced at being honoured by their good works’ [i.e., the good works of the ‘sanctified’]. St. Paul, so Bull affirmed, was contending for that faith which justifies, whereas St. James’s concern was for a confirmation of such faith by ‘good works’. The crucial point in both, according to Bull, was repentance.
Bull had been attacked in succession by Bishop George Morley (in a pastoral letter to the clergy of Winchester), Bishop Thomas Barlow of Lincoln (who lectured against Bull at Oxford), Dr. Thomas Tully, Charles Gataker, John Toombs, et al. He had answered with an Examen Censurae (1676) and, later, had been defended by Robert Nelson in his Life of Dr. George Bull (1713); see espec. pp. 90, 181, 211. Meanwhile, Bull had written a massive Defensio Fidei Nicaenae (1685) on which his subsequent fame largely rested. He ended his career as Bishop of St. David’s. It is worth remembering that Wesley had used Bull’s Companion for the Candidates of Holy Orders (published in 1714 after Bull’s death) as part of his own preparation for ordination as deacon in Sept. 1725. O who shall be able to stand, if this eminent scholar, Christian, and prelate, in his youth [04:397]wrote and published to the world, and in his riper years defended, the positions that follow!
The following page in the manuscript was first left blank, presumably for an English translation of Bull’s text, which is transcribed in Wesley’s Latin sermon. In AM, Clarke had supplied the English version here printed in square brackets. Sometime in the interval the blank page was numbered ‘10’ and Wesley had written in the following: ‘I shall be easily pardoned for adding but one more, but one also concerning whom almost the greatest among us might say, At his feet may I be found in the day of the Lord Jesus. His words are these:…’.
[‘A man is said (ἐξ ἔργων δικαιοῦται)
See Jas. 2:24. “to be justified by works”, because good works are the condition, according to the divine appointment, established in the gospel covenant, requisite and necessary to a man’s justification; that is, to his obtaining remission of sins through Christ.’
Bulli Harm. Apost., p. 4 [i.e., I.1.8; but cf. Bull’s own full text in No. 151, and note Bull’s context, a discussion of repentance].
A little after, being about to produce testimonies in proof of this proposition, he says, ‘The first class of these shall be those who speak of good works in a general sense, as the requisite and necessary condition of justification.’ Then follow certain texts of Scripture, after which he adds, ‘Who does not believe that in these Scriptures there is an abundance of good works required, which if a man do not perform he is altogether excluded from the hope of pardon, and remission of sins?’
Ibid., p. 8 [i.e., I.ii.3],
Having introduced some other things, he adds, ‘Besides faith, there is no one but may see that repentance is required as necessary to justification.
For Wesley’s not dissimilar view of the correlation of repentance and justifying faith, cf. No. 7, ‘The Way to the Kingdom’, II.1 and n. Now repentance is not one work alone, but is, as it were, a collection of many others, for in its compass the following works are comprehended: (1) sorrow on account of sin; (2) humiliation under the hand of God; (3) hatred to sin; (4) confession of sin; (5) ardent supplication of the divine mercy; (6) the love of God; (7) ceasing from sin; (8) firm purpose of new obedience; (9) restitution of ill-gotten goods; (10) forgiving our neighbour his transgressions against us; (11) works of beneficence, or almsgiving. How much these things avail to procure remission of sins from God is sufficiently evident from Daniel 4:27, where the prophet gives this wholesome advice to Nebuchadnezzar, who was at that time cleaving to his sins:
“Redeem your sins by almsgiving, and your iniquities by showing mercy to the poor.”’
Ibid., p. 10 [i.e., I.ii.6-7; cf. Wesley’s quotation of Bull’s Latin against Bull’s actual words].]
8. To instance in one point more. All the liturgy of the Church is full of petitions for that holiness without which the Scripture everywhere declares, no man shall see the Lord.
Heb. 12:14. And these are all summed up in those comprehensive words which we are supposed to be so frequently repeating, ‘Cleanse the thoughts of our hearts, by the inspiration of thy Holy Spirit, that we may perfectly love thee, and worthily magnify thy holy name.’
BCP, Communion, Collect for Purity. It is evident that in the last clause of this petition all outward holiness is contained; neither can it be carried to a greater height, or expressed in stronger terms. And those words, ‘cleanse the thoughts of our hearts,’ contain the negative branch of inward holiness, the height and depth of which is purity of heart by the inspiration of God’s Holy Spirit.
For Wesley’s mature doctrine of the distinction (and correlation) between inward and outward holiness, see No. 7, ‘The Way to the Kingdom’, I.10 and n. The remaining words, ‘that we may perfectly love thee’, contain the positive part of holiness, seeing this love, which is the fulfilling of the law,
Rom. 13:10. implies the whole mind that was in Christ.
See Phil. 2:5.
9. But now how does the general stream of writers and preachers (let me be excused the invidious task of instancing in particular persons) agree with this doctrine? Indeed, not at all. Very few can we find who simply and earnestly enforce it. But very many who write or preach as if Christian holiness or religion were a purely negative thing; as if not to curse or swear, not to lie or slander, not to be a drunkard, a thief, or an whoremonger, not to speak or do evil, was religion enough to entitle a man to heaven! How many, if they go something further than this, describe it only as an outward thing! As if it consisted chiefly, if not wholly, in doing good (as it is called) and using the means of grace! Or should they go further still, yet what do they add to this poor account of religion? Why, perhaps that a man should be orthodox in his opinions, and have a zeal for the constitution in church and state. And this is all! This is all the religion they can allow without [04:399]degenerating into enthusiasm! So true is it that the faith of a devil and the life of a heathen
See No. 1, Salvation by Faith, I.1, 2 and nn. make up what most men call a good Christian!
10. But why should we seek further witnesses of this? Are there not many present here who are of the same opinion? Who believe that a good moral man and a good Christian mean the same thing?
See No. 80, ‘On Friendship with the World’, §21 and n. That a man need not trouble himself any further if he only practises as much Christianity as was writ over the heathen emperor’s gate—‘Do as thou wouldst be done unto’?
Alexander Severus; see Nos. 2, The Almost Christian, I.5 and n.; and 30, ‘Sermon on the Mount, X’, §22 and n. Especially if he be not an infidel or an heretic, but believes all that the Bible and the church say is true!
11. I would not be so understood as if I despised these things; as [if] I undervalued either right opinions, true morality, or a zealous regard for the constitution we have received from our fathers. But yet, what are these things, being alone? What will they profit us in that day? What will it avail to tell the Judge of all, Lord, I was not as other men were, not unjust, not an adulterer, not a liar, not an immoral man?
See Luke 18:11. Yea, what will it avail if we have done all good, as well as done no harm—if we have given all our goods to feed the poor, and have not charity?
See 1 Cor. 13:3. How shall we then look on those who taught us to sleep on and take our rest,
See Mark 14:41. though the love of the Father was not in us? Or who teaching us to seek salvation by works cut us off from receiving that faith freely, whereby alone the true love of God could have been shed abroad in our hearts?
Rom. 5:5.
II. To these miserable corrupters of the gospel of Christ, and the poison they have spread abroad, is it in great measure owing that we [are] generally corrupted in practice as well as in doctrine; that there is hardly to be found among us (O tell it not in Gath! Publish it not in the streets of Ashkelon!)
2 Sam. 1:20. either the form of godliness or the power.
See 2 Tim. 3:5. So is the faithful city become an harlot.
1. With grief of heart I speak it, and not with joy, that scarce is the form of godliness seen among us. We are all indeed ‘called to [04:400]be saints’,
Rom. 1:7. and the name of Christians means no less. But who has so much as the appearance? Take anyone you meet. Take the second, third, fourth—the twentieth. Not one of them has even the appearance of a saint, any more than of an angel. Observe his look, his air, his gesture. Does it breathe nothing but God? Does it bespeak a temple of the Holy Ghost? Observe his conversation. Not an hour only, but day by day. Can you gather from any outward sign that God dwelleth in his heart? That this is an everlasting spirit who is going to God?
See Wesley’s Preface (1746), §5 and n. Would you imagine the blood of God was shed for that soul, and had purchased everlasting salvation for it, and that the spirit of God was now waiting till that salvation should be wrought out with fear and trembling?
See Phil. 2:12.
2. Should it be said, ‘Why, what signifies the form of godliness?’ we readily answer, Nothing, if [it] be alone. But the absence of the form signifies much. It infallibly proves the absence of the power. For though the form may be without the power, yet the power cannot be without the form.
See 2 Tim. 3:5; see also below, II.3-5, where Wesley concedes that many of the ritual forms of Christian worship continue to be observed, in some degree, in the colleges and the university. E.g., the brothers Wesley and the Oxford Methodists had themselves taken full advantage of the ‘forms’ of university sermons, etc. See No. 2, The Almost Christian, I.(II).4 and n. Outward religion may be where inward is not. But if there is none without there can be none within.
3. But it may be said, ‘We have public prayers both morning and evening in all our societies.’
As may be inferred from the Latin text, this is not a reference to religious societies in the Church of England (like those of Horneck and Woodward in Westminster and London—e.g., Fetter Lane) but the colleges and houses of the university, each of which was a societas academica with rector (or ‘president’, ‘master’, ‘dean’), fellows, scholars, and pupils. Each such society had its own chapel (or, in Christ Church, a cathedral) with regular prayers and eucharists; cf. Hastings Rashdall, The Universities of Europe in the Middle Ages (Oxford, 1951), III.221, 374, 400-401. It is true; and it were to be wished that all the members thereof, more especially the elder, and those of note and character, would by constantly attending them show how sensible they are of that invaluable privilege. But have all who attend them the very form of godliness? Before those solemn addresses to God begin, does the behaviour of all who are present show that they know before whom they stand? What impression appears to be left on their mind when those holy [04:401]offices are ended? And even during their continuance,
At this point, Wesley wrote, then deleted, ‘(God knoweth the heart, but we speak now only of outward things)’. can it be reasonably inferred from the tenor of their outward behaviour that their hearts are earnestly fixed on him who standeth in the midst of them?
See Luke 24:36, etc. I much fear, were a heathen that understood not our tongue to come into one of these our assemblies he would suspect nothing less than that we were pouring out our hearts before the Majesty of heaven and earth. What then shall we say, if indeed God is not mocked, but, what a man soweth, that also shall he reap.
See Gal. 6:7.
4. On Sundays, however, say some, it cannot be denied that we have the form of godliness, having sermons preached both morning and afternoon, over and above the morning and evening service. But do we keep the rest of the sabbath day holy? Is there no needless visiting upon it? No trifling? No impertinence of conversation? Do you neither yourself do unnecessary work upon it, nor suffer any others over whom you have any power to break the laws both of God and man herein? If you do, even in this you have nothing whereof to boast;
At this point, Wesley wrote, then deleted, ‘God be merciful to thee a sinner.’ herein also you are guilty before God.
5. But if we have the form of godliness on one day in a week, is there not on other days what is quite contrary thereto? Are not the best of our conversing hours spent in foolish talking and jesting, which are not convenient?
Eph. 5:4. Nay, perhaps in wanton talking
In his Latin text, Wesley cites the orig. Greek of Col. 3:8, αἰσχρολογία, i.e., ‘filthy communication’ (AV). too, such as modest ears could not bear. Are there not κώμοι καὶ πότοι
See 1 Pet. 4:3: ‘carousals and drinking bouts’. among us? And glorying in this our shame?
See Phil. 3:19. Yea, are not many among us found to eat and drink with the drunken?
Matt. 24:49. And if so, what marvel is it that our profaneness should also go up into the heavens, and our oaths and curses enter into the ears of the Lord of Sabaoth!
6. And even as to the hours more immediately assigned for studying, are they generally spent to any better purpose? Not if they are employed, as is too common, in reading news, plays, or [04:402]idle tales,
See No. 4, Scriptural Christianity, IV.9, where Wesley denounces the worshippers at St. Mary’s for ‘wasting away [the time] day after day, either in reading what has no tendency to Christianity, or in gaming, or in—you know not what’. Yet his own reading list for Sept. 1729, includes a general entry, ‘novels’, and frequent reading of plays (which he later put to good use as illustrations in his sermons). which naturally tend to increase our native corruption and heat the furnace of our unholy desires seven times hotter than it was before.
See Dan. 3:19. How little preferable is this to the laborious idleness of those who spend day after day in gaming or diversions! Vilely casting away that time the value of which they cannot know till they are passed through it into eternity.
See Law, Serious Call, ch. i, pp. 7-14.
7. Know ye not then so much as this, you that are called moral men, that all idleness is immorality? That there is no grosser dishonesty than sloth? That every (voluntary) blockhead is a knave? He defrauds his benefactors, his parents, and the world, and robs both God and his own soul. Yet how many of these are among us! How many lazy drones, as if only
fruges consumere nati!
Horace, Epistles, I.ii.27 (‘born to consume the produce [of others]’).
How many whose ignorance is not owing to incapacity, but to mere laziness! How few (let it not seem immodest that even such an one as I should touch on that tender point) of the vast number who have it in their power are truly learned men! Not to speak of the other eastern tongues, who (almost) is there that can be said to understand Hebrew? Might I not say, or even Greek? A little of Homer or Xenophon we may still remember; but how few can readily read and understand so much as a page of Clemens Alexandrinus, St. Chrysostom, or Ephraem Syrus?
See Address to the Clergy, I.2. And as to philosophy (not to mention mathematics or the abstruser branches of it) how few do we find who have laid the very foundation, who are masters even of logic! Who throughly understand so much as the rules of syllogizing! The very doctrine of the moods and figures!
Wesley’s hearers would have realized that he had been ‘moderator of the classes’ (i.e., ‘logic-master’) at Lincoln. Oh! what is so scarce as learning, but religion!
8. And indeed learning will be seldom found without religion. For temporal views, as experience shows, will very rarely suffice [04:403]to carry anyone through the labour required to the being a thorough scholar. Can it then be dissembled that there is too often a defect in those to whom the care of youth is entrusted? Is that solemn direction sufficiently considered, ‘Tutor scholares regimini suo commissos, probis moribus imbuat, et maxime in rudimentis religionis et doctrinae articulis’?
Statut., p. 7. [Wesley’s text here and in the following pages is an abridgement of excerpts from the earlier (Laudian) statutes of Oxford University, published frequently from 1671 onwards as Parecbolae; sive, Excerpta e Corpore Statutorum Universitatis Oxoniensis. Accedunt Articuli Religionis XXXIX in Ecclesia Anglicana recepti…. The actual text reads: Tutor vero Scholares Tutelae et regimini suo commissos probis moribus imbuat, et in probatis authoribus instituat: et maxime in rudimentibus Religionis et doctrinae Articulis in synodo.—‘Let each tutor carefully imbue those scholars committed to his tutelage with proper morals and ground them in respect for constituted authorities—and especially in the rudiments of religion and the official doctrines of the Articles.’] Do they to whom this important charge is given labour diligently to lay this good foundation? To fix true principles of religion in the minds of the youth entrusted with them by their lectures? To recommend the practice thereof by the powerful and pleasing influence of their examples? To enforce this by frequent private advice, earnestly and strongly inculcated? To observe the progress, and carefully inquire into the behaviour of every one of them? In a word, to watch over their souls, as they that must give account?
Heb. 13:17.
9. Suffer me, since I have begun to speak on this head, to go yet a little further. Is there sufficient care taken that they should know and keep the statutes which we are all engaged to observe? How then is it that they are so notoriously broken every day? To instance only in a few:
Statutum est, quod ad officia divina, et conciones publice habendas, omnes—graduati et scholares—diligenter accedant, et eisdem debita cum reverentia, quoad peractae fuerint, a principio usque ad finem intersint.
P. 181. [The actual text reads: Statutum est, quod ad Officia Divina sive Preces solemnes iuxta Liturgiam Ecclesiae Anglicanae, et Conciones publice coram Universitate habendas, omnes Doctores, Magistri, Graduati et Scholares, diligenter accedant et eisdem debita cum reverentia et attentione, quoad peractae fuerint, a principio usque ad finem intersint.—‘It is prescribed that, with respect to divine services and solemn prayers according to the liturgy of the Church of England, and also the public sermons delivered before the University, all doctors, masters, graduates, and scholars shall be present at them from the beginning to the end, with due reverence and attention, until they all be finished.’]
Statutum est, quod omnes (exceptis filiis baronum) vestibus coloris nigri aut subfusci se assuefaciant: nec quae fastum aut luxum prae se ferunt imitentur, sed ab iis procul absint.
P. 157. [Statutum est, quod omnes Praefecti, Collegiorum Socii et Scholares, necnon omnes Sacris Ordinibus initiati, prout Clerios decet, vestiantur; et ea observent, quae Canonicis Sanctionibus praecipiuntur. Quodque alii omnes (exceptis filiis Baronum in Superiore Parliamenti Domo suffragii ius habentium) vestibus coloris nigri aut subfusci se assuefaciant: nec quae fastum aut luxum prae se ferunt, imitentur: sed ab iis procul absint.—‘It is prescribed that all Prefects, Fellows and Scholars of Colleges, as well as all in Holy Orders, as befits their clerical rank, shall be properly clothed; and that all canonical sanctions in this matter shall be duly observed. Moreover [it is enacted that] all others (the sons of the nobility of the Upper House of Parliament being excepted) shall customarily wear black or dark coloured clothes; and that they should not imitate any style of clothes that bespeaks arrogance or luxury, but rather to avoid such things from afar.’]
Statutum est, quod scholares cuiuscunque conditionis, abstineant ab omni lusus genere, in quo de pecunia concertatur; veluti a lusu talorum, alearum, et chartarum pictarum, nec non a lusu globorum nec huius modi publicis lusibus intersint.
P. 166. [Statutum est, quod Scholares, cuiuscunque conditionis, abstineant ab omni lusus genere, in quo de pecunia concertatur; veluti a lusu Talorum, Alearum, et Chartarum Pictarum, nec non a lusu Globorum, in privatis Oppidanorum areis hortisque: nec huius modi publicis lusibus, per Statuta Regni prohibitis, intersint.—‘It is prescribed that scholars, of whatever rank, shall abstain from every kind of game in which one plays for money, such as games of dice, gambling, or cards; further from ball games played on private property, nor should they attend such games, which are prohibited by royal decree.’]
Statutum est quod scholares cuiuscunque conditionis, a diversoriis, cauponiis, oenopoliis, ac domibus quibuscunque intra civitatem in quibus vinum aut quivis alius potus…ordinarie venditur, abstineant.
P. 164. [Statutum est, quod Scholares cuiuscunque conditionis, a Diversoriis, Cauponiis, Oenopoliis, ac domibus quibuscunque intra Civitatem vel Praecinctum Universitatis, in quibus vinum, aut quivis alius potus, aut herba Nicotiniana sive Tobacco, ordinarie venditur, abstineant.—‘It is prescribed that all scholars, of whatever rank, abstain from frequenting inns, taverns, wine shops, and all houses, whether within the City [of Oxford] or the precincts of the university, where wine or other drinks, or the herb nicotiniana (or tobacco) are regularly sold.’]
10. It will perhaps be objected, ‘These are but little things.’ Nay, but perjury is not a little thing: nor consequently the wilful breach of any rule which we have solemnly sworn to observe. Surely those who speak thus have forgotten those words, ‘Tu fidem dabis ad observandum omnia Statuta huius universitatis—ita Deus te adiuvet, tactis Sacrosanctis Christi Evangeliis.’
P. 229. [Tu fidem dabis ad Observandum omnia Statuta, Privilegia, et Consuetudinis huius Universitatis Oxoniensis. Ita Deus te adiuvet, tactis Sacrosanctis Christi Evangeliis.—‘You shall pledge your faith to the observance of all the statutes, privileged rights and duties, and the established customs of this University of Oxford. So help you God, since you have made this oath with your hand on the Holy Gospels of Christ.’]
11. But is this oath sufficiently considered by those who take it? Or any of those prescribed by public authority? Is not this solemn act of religion, the calling God to record on our souls, commonly treated as a slight thing? In particular by those who swear by the living God, ‘quod nec prece nec pretio, nec odio, nec amicitia,
nec timore, nec spe testimonium indigno cuivis perhibebunt’?
P. 88. [Magistro…tu iurabis, quod nec prece, nec pretio, nec odio, nec amicitia, nec timore, nec spe testimonium indigno cuivis perhibebis dignove denegabis.—‘As a teacher, you have sworn that you will not be swayed by entreaties or bribes, nor by hatred or friendship, nor by fear or hope, to give a testimonial for any unworthy person or against any worthy one.’] And by those who swear, ‘Scio hunc aptum et idoneum esse moribus et scientia ad eum gradum ad quem praesentatur’?
P. 114. [Hi Deponentes, a Bedello Facultatis admoniti, et si opus fuerit, nominatim vocati, si gillatim coram Vice-Cancellario inter Procuratores in genus decumbentes, submissa voce, nequis praeterea exudiat, hac iur amenti formula onerabuntur. (Dom. Doctor, Magister, vel Domine) Tu dices fide tua data huic Universitati utrum scias, credas, vel nescias, hunc vel hos Praesentatos, aptum vel aptos et idoneos esse moribus et scientia, ad eum gradum ad quem praesentatur, sub Forma qua praesentatur. Cui quilibet secreto repondebit per verbum, Scio, Nescio vel Credo.—(The options in responding to the formal inquiry of the university officials as to the intellectual aptitudes and moral character of a graduand): ‘I know’; ‘I do not know’; ‘I believe’.] It is probably to this latter case that the explicatio iuramenti
‘What it means to take an oath’. has an immediate reference, in that clause, ‘Intenditur, periurio se obligare…affirmantes in luramentis assertoriis, se aliquid…scire, credereve, quod non sciverint, crediderintve.’
P. 200. [Intenditur igitur periurio se obligare, primo, delinquentes contra Statuta sub poena peri urii sanctita, out contra Statuta ad quae speciatim observanda fide sua data Universitati obstringuntur ut in luramentis assertoriis, affirmantes se aliquid per Statuta requisitum fecisse quod non fecerintvel scire credereve, quod non sciverim, crediderintve.—‘It is, therefore, a case of perjury, in the first instance, for anyone to disregard the holy statute [against misrepresentation] to which one has subscribed under pain of perjury, or the statute which defines the faith owed to the University, whenever one swears, by assertion or affirmation, in any case covered by these statutes, as if they knew or believed anything when they did not, or did not know or believed something when they did.’ Wesley’s abridgement focuses on the intention of the oath: ‘It is defined as a case of perjury for anyone to affirm, in a sworn declaration, that he knows or believes something that he did not know or believe.’]
12. Yet one thing more. We have all testified before God that all and every [one of] the Articles of our Church, as also the Book of Common Prayer and the Ordering of Bishops, Priests, and Deacons, are agreeable to the Word of God.
Wesley is repeating one of the variant forms by which clergy subscribed to the Thirty-nine Articles and Liturgy on receiving a licence to preach, on being ordained, and on other occasions; cf. Arts. XXXIV, XXXV, XXXVI. And in so doing we have likewise testified that both the First and Second Book of Homilies doth contain godly and wholesome doctrine.
An inference from any subscription to Art. XXXV (‘Of Homilies’) of the Thirty-nine Articles. But upon what evidence have many of us declared this? Have we not affirmed the things we know not? If so, however true they may happen to be, we are found false witnesses before God. Have the
greater part of us ever used any means to know whether these things were so or not? Have we ever for one hour seriously considered the Articles to which we have subscribed? If not, how shamefully do we elude the design of the wise compilers, who compiled them ‘ad tollendam opinionum dissentionem et consensum in vera religione firmandum’!
Wesley’s version from the Preface to the Articuli of 1562 (pub. 1563): ad tollendam opinionum dissensionem, et firmandum in vera religione consensum. The authorized English translation (1571): ‘for the avoiding of the diversities of opinions, and for the stablishing of consent touching true Religion’. It is ironic that, given his audience, Wesley had not verified the original; cf. Philip Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom, III.487. Have one half of us read over the Book of Common Prayer, and of Ordering Bishops, Priests, and Deacons?
The Ordinal (‘being the Form of Making, Ordaining, and Consecrating Bishops, Priests, and Deacons’) appears as an addendum to the BCP. If not, what is it we have so solemnly confirmed? In plain terms, we cannot tell. And as to the two Books of Homilies, it is well if a tenth part of those who have subscribed to them, I will not say, had considered them before they did this, but if they have even read them over to this day! Alas, my brethren! How shall we reconcile these things even to common honesty, to plain heathen morality? So far are those who do them, nay, and perhaps defend them too, from having the very form of Christian godliness.
13. But waiving all these things, where is the power? Where are the living witnesses of this? Who among us (let God witness with our hearts) experimentally know the force of inward holiness? Who ‘feels in himself the working of the Spirit of Christ, drawing up his mind to high and heavenly things’?
Cf. Art. XVII (‘Of Predestination and Election’). Who can witness, ‘The thoughts of my heart God hath cleansed, by the inspiration of his Holy Spirit’?
Cf. BCP, Communion, Collect for Purity. Who knoweth that peace of God that passeth all understanding?
Phil. 4:7. Who is he that rejoiceth, with joy unspeakable and full of glory?
1 Pet. 1:8. Whose affections are set on things above, not on things of the earth? Whose life is hid with Christ in God?
See Col. 3:2-3. Who can say: ‘I am crucified with Christ. But I live. Yet not I, but Christ liveth in me. And the life that I now live in the flesh, I live by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me.’
Gal. 2:20. In whose heart is the love of God shed abroad, by the Holy Ghost given unto him!
See Rom. 5:5.
14. Is not almost the very notion of this religion lost? Is there not a gross, overflowing ignorance of it? Nay, is it not utterly despised? Is it not wholly set at nought, trodden under foot? Were anyone to witness these things before God, would he not be accounted a madman, an enthusiast? Am not I unto you as a barbarian while I speak thus?
See 1 Cor. 14:11. My brethren, my heart bleeds for you. O that ye would at length take knowledge, and understand that these are the words of truth and soberness! O that ye would know,
Wesley first wrote, then deleted, ‘that ye would know, I am not mad, though I thus speak’; cf. No. 142, ‘The Wisdom of Winning Souls’, I, n. 18. at least in this your day, the things that make for your peace!
See Luke 19:42. Wesley intended to close at this point, for in the MS there was the beginning of an ascription. This is crossed out, to be started again at §16, a rather peculiar hortation and blessing.
15. I have been a messenger of heavy tidings this day. But the love of Christ constrained me:
See 2 Cor. 5:14. and to me it was the less grievous because for you it was safe.
See Phil 3:1. I desire not to accuse the children of my people.
See Ezek. 33:2, 12. Therefore, neither do I speak thus in the ears of them that sit on the wall.
See 2 Kgs. 18:27; Isa. 36:12. But to you I endeavour to speak the truth in love,
See Eph. 4:15. as a faithful minister of Jesus Christ.
See Col. 1:7; 1 Tim. 4:6. And I can now call you to record this day, that I am pure from the blood of all men. For I have not shunned to declare unto you, all the counsel of God.
Acts 20:26-27.
16. May the God of all grace,
1 Pet. 5:10. who is long-suffering, of tender mercy, and repenteth him of the evil, fix these things in your hearts, and water the seed he hath sown with the dew of heaven! May he correct whatsoever he seeth amiss in us! May he supply whatsoever is wanting! May he perfect that which is according to his will, and so establish, strengthen, settle us,
See 1 Pet. 5:10. that this place may again be a faithful city to her Lord, yea, the praise of the whole earth!
